item.title: Saving More for 2027: What Retirement Limit Adjustments Could Mean for Your 401(k) and IRA
item.body:
Every fall, the Internal Revenue Service publishes cost-of-living adjustments for the coming year, including the contribution limits for workplace retirement plans and individual retirement accounts. Because many of these limits are indexed to inflation, they tend to creep up over time. This guide explains how the limits work, which numbers to watch, and who is actually in a position to use the extra room.

*Note: This article is general information, not tax, legal or investment advice. The 2027 figures should be confirmed against the IRS announcement. The figures below for 2026 are the most recent published baseline, so use them as a reference point.*

## How the annual adjustments work

Congress sets the formulas, and the IRS applies inflation data to them. A few key points:

- **Indexing is not automatic for every limit.** Many caps rise only once inflation pushes the calculation past a rounding threshold. The 401(k) deferral limit is adjusted in $500 steps, while the IRA limit moves in $500 steps as well, so a modest rise in prices may produce no change at all in some years.
- **Announcements usually arrive in October or November.** Employers and payroll providers then update their systems, often in time for the new year.
- **Limits apply per person, not per account.** The 401(k) employee deferral limit is shared across all of your workplace plans of the same type. The IRA limit is shared across all of your traditional and Roth IRAs.

## The 2026 baseline

For reference, these are the 2026 figures that the 2027 numbers will build on:

| Item | 2026 limit |
|---|---|
| 401(k), 403(b), most 457 plans: employee deferral | $24,500 |
| Catch-up contribution, age 50 and older | $8,000 |
| Higher catch-up, ages 60 to 63 | $11,250 |
| IRA contribution limit | $7,500 |
| IRA catch-up, age 50 and older | $1,100 |
| SIMPLE IRA employee deferral | $17,000 |

If the 2027 adjustments follow the usual pattern, expect modest increases in some of these lines and no change in others.

## Catch-up contributions: what to know

Catch-up contributions let older savers put away more than the standard limit. Two features deserve attention.

**The ages 60 to 63 window.** Under the SECURE 2.0 Act, workers who turn 60, 61, 62 or 63 during the year may be eligible for a higher catch-up amount than the standard age-50 catch-up. It is available only if your plan has adopted it, so check with your plan administrator.

**Roth treatment for higher earners.** Beginning in 2026, workers whose prior-year wages from the employer sponsoring the plan exceeded a set threshold (indexed from $145,000, and $150,000 for 2026) must make their catch-up contributions on a Roth, or after-tax, basis. That means no upfront tax deduction, but qualified withdrawals can be tax-free later. If your plan does not offer a Roth option, affected workers may not be able to make catch-up contributions at all, so it is worth asking.

## Income thresholds: who can use the extra room

Raising a cap does not help if your income or your plan features keep you from using it. Several thresholds matter.

**Traditional IRA deductions.** If you or your spouse is covered by a workplace plan, the deduction for traditional IRA contributions phases out at certain income levels. For 2026, the range for single filers covered by a workplace plan is $81,000 to $91,000 of modified adjusted gross income. For married couples filing jointly where the contributing spouse is covered, it is $129,000 to $149,000.

**Roth IRA eligibility.** The ability to contribute directly to a Roth IRA phases out at higher incomes. For 2026, the range is $153,000 to $168,000 for single filers and $242,000 to $252,000 for married couples filing jointly.

**The Saver's Credit.** Lower- and moderate-income workers may qualify for a tax credit of up to 50% of a limited amount of retirement contributions. Income limits rise each year with inflation, so a higher threshold can bring new households into eligibility.

When these income ranges move up, more households can deduct IRA contributions or contribute to a Roth IRA, even if the headline dollar limit stays the same.

## Who can realistically use the higher limits

The honest answer is that most workers do not reach the maximums. Industry data on plan participants consistently shows that only a small share of savers contribute the full amount allowed. Higher limits are most relevant to:

- **High earners** who already max out their accounts and want more tax-advantaged space.
- **Workers over 50**, who tend to have more disposable income and a shorter runway to retirement.
- **Households with a plan that allows extra features**, such as after-tax contributions or in-plan Roth conversions.

For everyone else, the more useful step may be raising a contribution rate by one or two percentage points rather than aiming for the cap.

## Practical steps before January

1. **Check your current contribution rate.** Compare what you contribute to the limit and see how much room you have.
2. **Capture the employer match first.** Free matching dollars generally come before any other savings goal.
3. **Ask about plan features.** Find out whether your plan offers Roth contributions, catch-up contributions, and the ages 60 to 63 option.
4. **Plan for the Roth catch-up rule** if your wages are near the threshold.
5. **Set up automatic increases.** Many plans can raise your contribution rate annually, which makes use of new room without extra effort.
6. **Review your tax situation.** A tax professional can help you decide between pre-tax and Roth contributions based on your current and expected future bracket.

## Bottom line

The yearly adjustment is a small but useful opportunity. Whether the new limits matter to you depends less on the headline numbers and more on your income, your age, and what your plan allows. Once the IRS publishes the official 2027 figures, compare them with your current contribution settings and adjust early in the year, when you have the most time to spread contributions across paychecks.
